description: Hi, I’m shanza, a mobile and web developer building AI-powered apps.I build with Flutter, web technologies, and Ai, including agentic AI workflows and prompt engineering. I like turning complicated technology into something people can understand and use in seconds, and that’s exactly what I want to do with this challenge.Building “Earth Choreographer” for Dancing with the SARs,an interactive globe that turns NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data into simple visual “dance moves” of Earth’s changing surface.
summary: Quetta Valley | NISAR radar explorer is an open-source interactive web map that turns NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data into a story anyone can explore. We chain nine consecutive L-band interferograms (20 Jun to 18 Oct 2026) into cumulative line-of-sight (LOS) change over Quetta valley, Pakistan. Users can play a timeline, hover to read values, and click any spot to see how it changed. The project addresses the challenge by making complex radar measurements understandable without radar expertise. It is also honest about uncertainty: the data are Provisional, about 2-3 cm of noise remains, and the sign convention is not confirmed, so the map highlights candidate areas for closer study instead of claiming ground subsidence. It shows how open NISAR data can become an accessible tool for non-experts.
details:
project details:

What it does: A static web app shows NISAR radar-derived relative line-of-sight (LOS) change over Quetta valley across 10 dates (20 Jun - 18 Oct 2026). Users play a timeline, hover for values, click a spot for a time-series chart, and switch between dark and satellite basemaps.

How it works: (1) We searched NISAR L2 GUNW (Provisional) products with asf_search and chose track 92, frame 73 (descending, L-band HH), which fully covers our study box and has nine consecutive pairs. (2) In Python (h5py, NumPy, pyproj) we crop each pair, mask pixels with coherence <= 0.5 or outside the main unwrapped component, subtract the ionospheric phase screen, remove the median of valid pixels of each pair, convert phase to centimeters (about 1.94 cm per radian) and add the pairs up over time. (3) We export a 160 x 160 lon/lat grid, color overlay images and a JSON data cube. (4) A static site (MapLibre GL JS, Chart.js, GitHub Pages) displays it.

Tools: Python, Google Colab, asf_search, h5py, NumPy, pyproj, Matplotlib; HTML/CSS/JavaScript, MapLibre GL JS, Chart.js; GitHub Pages.

Creativity and impact: the timeline places each date at its real position in time, the interface is built for non-experts, and the project is deliberately transparent about uncertainty.

Limitations: Provisional data; 2-3 cm of noise in apparently stable areas; no troposphere or solid Earth tide correction yet; regional median reference; one track (LOS only); sign convention not confirmed; four months is a short record. Next steps: confirm the sign convention, apply correction layers, choose a validated stable reference, add ascending tracks.
